title: A Room in Mithadar, Benches on the Pavement and One Old Van
dek: In 1951 Abdul Sattar Edhi opened a free dispensary in a tiny Karachi shop, slept on a bench outside it, and in 1957 put an old van to work as an ambulance.

story.event: Opening a free dispensary in Mithadar, Karachi, in 1951 and acquiring a first ambulance in 1957
story.summary: In 1951 Abdul Sattar Edhi, who had migrated to Karachi in 1947, used his savings to open a free dispensary in a tiny shop in Mithadar, sleeping on a bench outside it. During the 1957 Asian flu epidemic he treated the sick in tents, and a businessman's donation let him buy an old van that he drove as his first ambulance; the work grew into the Edhi Foundation, which by his death in 2016 ran about 1,500 ambulances.
paragraphs: Abdul Sattar Edhi reached Karachi in 1947, part of the mass migration of Muslims from India after partition. He had been nursing his mother, who was paralysed, and he later said that caring for her "made me ponder the misery of others who suffered". It was a time when most medicine was out of reach for the poor. Half a century on, he said the satisfaction of caring for her had never ended.

His first dispensary was a shared one, set up with others from his Memon community, and the Magsaysay foundation records that he grew frustrated with his associates' caution. In 1951 he used his savings to buy a tiny shop in Mithadar, a poor quarter of old Karachi, and opened a free dispensary of his own with a doctor who taught him the basics. To be on hand at all hours, he slept on a cement bench outside. A banner hung at the door: "Those who give charity are blessed, those who do not are also blessed." Donors got a receipt and could have their money back if they changed their minds.

"I saw people lying on the pavement," he told NPR in 2009, recalling his early years. Flu had spread and nobody was treating the sick, so he set out benches and persuaded medical students to volunteer. Penniless, he begged in the street, "and people gave." When an Asian flu epidemic swept Karachi in 1957, he put up tents to treat people, asking them to pay only if they could. "It was the first mass recognition of my work," he later said. A businessman from his own Memon community then made a single large gift, 20,000 rupees by the Balzan Foundation's account, and Edhi bought an old van to serve as an ambulance. He drove it himself.

The van was in constant use, and a few volunteers joined him. He refused money from governments, relying, he said, on his own countrymen alone. The trust he built became the Edhi Foundation in 1974, and by his death in July 2016 it ran about 1,500 ambulances. He said he owned nothing but two sets of clothes and the small room his mother had left him, in the alley where he began.

quote.text: a man when he has done a good act does not call out for others to come and see, but he goes on to another act, as a vine goes on to produce again the grapes in season.
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Edhi's work was less one founding act than the same act repeated: another patient, another drive, another donor's coin. Marcus Aurelius pictures that kind of goodness as a vine's, which does not announce its grapes and bears again, but in season.

reflection: Edhi's start was small enough to be almost invisible: a room, a doctor on a wage, benches on a pavement, one old van. What turned it into an institution was repetition, and other people joining once they had seen it work.

Marcus Aurelius's vine is a good picture of that, with one detail worth keeping: it bears fruit in season, not all year round. Edhi chose to live without a home outside his dispensary. That was his choice, and it is not a pattern you need to follow. You can take the steadiness from his story and leave the sleeplessness. The vine rests too.
invitation: Think of one small service you do so regularly that nobody, you included, notices it any more. Do it today without mentioning it, and notice how it feels.

sources.title: Abdul Sattar Edhi: 2000 Balzan Prize for Humanity, Peace and Fraternity among Peoples (prizewinner profile)
sources.supports: In 1951 Edhi bought a small shop in Mithadar from his savings and opened his own dispensary for everyone; the banner 'Those who give charity are blessed, those who do not are also blessed'; receipts and refunds for donors; cheaper medicines and a physician on a fixed salary; mornings in a doctor's clinic training in pharmacy and accountancy; the dispensary never shut and he had no home outside it; official recognition in connection with the 1957 flu epidemic; a businessman's donation of 20,000 rupees and the old van bought as an ambulance and in constant use; the Edhi Foundation established in 1974.

sources.title: Acceptance Speech, Rome, 15 November 2000
sources.publisher: International Balzan Prize Foundation (Abdul Sattar Edhi's own speech)
sources.supports: Edhi's own account: caring for his paralysed mother and the lasting satisfaction of it; the foundation began in an indigent area of Karachi as a free dispensary he 'rented and ran alone'; 'in the year 1957, we received one ambulance as a donation'; a few volunteers then joined; reliance only on his own countrymen and refusal of government and charity-organisation donations; Guinness record (2000) as the largest volunteer ambulance organisation; owning nothing except a small room his mother left him in the alley where he began and two pairs of clothing.

sources.title: Edhi, Abdul Sattar: 1986 Ramon Magsaysay Award for Public Service (biography and citation)
sources.supports: Migration to Pakistan with his family in 1947; his mother's paralysis two years later alerting him to the suffering of the sick when most medicine was unavailable; the Bantva Memon Dispensary established with colleagues in 1950; frustration with the conservatism of his associates; refusal of government assistance.

sources.title: Pakistan Philanthropist Cares For Karachi's Forgotten (Julie McCarthy, July 2009)
sources.supports: The eight-by-eight-foot room bought nearly 60 years earlier as a dispensary; arrival in Karachi with the migration of Muslims from India; Edhi's recollection: 'I saw people lying on the pavement', flu in Karachi with no one to treat the sick, benches and volunteer medical students, begging for donations in the street 'and people gave'.

sources.title: Abdul Sattar Edhi, Known As 'Pakistan's Mother Teresa,' Dies At 88 (Hannah Bloch, NPR, 8 July 2016)
sources.supports: Death in Karachi in July 2016 aged 88; a fleet of 1,500 ambulances; Edhi frequently drove his own ambulance; he started a clinic and a one-man ambulance service in Karachi; he accepted only private donations and refused government support.

sources.title: Angel of mercy (2016)
sources.supports: Death on 8 July 2016 at 88; about 1,500 ambulances; the NPR recollection of the flu, benches and begging; a makeshift hospital for victims of the 1957 flu epidemic.

sources.title: Humanitarian to a Nation: Abdul Sattar Edhi (Saudi Aramco World, November/December 2004; reprinted 2016)
sources.supports: In 1951, four years after the family moved to Karachi, Edhi used savings to buy a tiny shop less than three metres on a side in Mithadar and set up a free dispensary with a doctor who taught him the basics of health care; he slept on a cement bench outside it; caring for his mother made him think of the misery of others; in 1957 a flu epidemic swept Karachi and he set up tented camps on the outskirts; he returned a cheque from President Zia ul-Haq and refused government money.

sources.title: Abdul Sattar Edhi obituary (Jon Boone, 13 July 2016)
sources.supports: Moved to Pakistan in August 1947; charitable work expanded in the 1957 Asian flu epidemic, when he borrowed money for tents and asked people to contribute only if they could afford it; "It was the first mass recognition of my work"; a single donation from a businessman, a fellow Memon, paid for his first ambulance, which he drove himself; a fleet of 1,500 ambulances.

cross_checks.claim: In 1951 Edhi opened his own dispensary in a tiny shop in Mithadar, Karachi, bought with his savings.
During the 1957 flu epidemic in Karachi Edhi treated the sick in tents and his work won wide recognition.
A businessman's donation after the 1957 epidemic paid for Edhi's first ambulance, an old van, which he drove himself.
Edhi refused government money and relied on private donations.
By Edhi's death in July 2016 the foundation ran about 1,500 ambulances.

research_notes: Sources disagree on several early details, so the story keeps to what they share. Start of the dispensary: the 1986 Magsaysay biography says that in 1950 he set up the Bantva Memon Dispensary with colleagues and, frustrated by their conservatism, assumed full responsibility for it in 1953; the Balzan Foundation, AramcoWorld (2004) and the BBC (2016) date his own dispensary in Mithadar to 1951, and Balzan, AramcoWorld and NPR (2009) say he bought the small shop or room with his savings, while Edhi's own 2000 Balzan speech calls it a free dispensary he 'rented and ran alone'. The story uses 1951 and 'bought'. Free or cheap: AramcoWorld and Edhi say free; Balzan says medicines were sold below market price; the story says free. His mother: the Magsaysay biography dates her paralysis to two years after the 1947 migration, but AramcoWorld implies he was already caring for her as a schoolboy in India; the story gives no date. Room size: AramcoWorld says under three metres a side, NPR eight by eight feet, Edhi's 2000 speech a 10 by 10 room his mother left him; no size is given for the shop. 1957: AramcoWorld says he set up tented camps with his own money (and mentions free immunisations); the Guardian says he borrowed money for tents and asked people to pay only if they could; Khaleej Times says a makeshift hospital. The story says he put up tents without saying how they were paid for. First ambulance: Balzan says a businessman gave 20,000 rupees and he bought an old van; the Guardian says a single donation from a fellow Memon businessman bought it and that he drove it himself; Edhi said in 2000 that in 1957 'we received one ambulance as a donation'; Khaleej Times alone says the first ambulance was bought in 1965, which the story does not use. The 20,000 rupee figure is attributed to Balzan. The NPR flu recollection is undated in the transcript; the story presents it as his memory of his early years and dates only the 1957 epidemic separately. Ambulance numbers: about 400 (Edhi, 2000), up to 800 in the mid-1990s (Balzan), about 1,500 at his death (NPR 2016, the Guardian, Khaleej Times; Al Jazeera in 2017 gave more than 1,800); the story uses about 1,500. Ages vary between sources, so none is given. Dawn's 2016 obituary returns 403 to automated requests and is not cited. The Marcus Aurelius passage is applied by analogy.
